name: Islamic fundamentalism
summary: Islamic fundamentalism seeks a return to the original texts of Islam, the Quran and Sunnah, and the application of sharia as the basis of law and public life. Its adherents reject the separation of religion and state, secular democracy and Western cultural influence, and hold that sovereignty belongs to God alone. Strands differ on whether change should come by preaching, elections or armed jihad.
scope: Islamic fundamentalism as the defining sources describe it: the Muslim current that holds the Quran and Sunnah to give rules for all of social, political and economic life, presents Islam as a comprehensive system distinct from every other, and rejects Westernising modernists, secularists and nationalists (Shepard; Britannica). The core is the Sunni lay-revivalist line of Hasan al-Banna and the Muslim Brotherhood and Abul A'la Mawdudi (with Qutb's Milestones as a text the sources place in the same current), read as a text-first, sharia-first programme. Britannica also files Wahhabism, Salafism, the Taliban, Boko Haram and Iran's Principlists under the label and notes they differ widely (some use terrorism, some do not; some leftist, some free-market); those strands, Shi'i clerical rule and the Gulf monarchies' state religion are not represented here. Modernist Islam is excluded.
